records.bodyText:
This smacks of extreme desperation from the wind industry as it watches in horror as their cash cow is dragged step by painfully slow step to the public money abattoir to be put out of OUR misery.

As politicians are forced kicking and screaming into the realisation that building wind turbines so remotely and so far from the point of need is perhaps not such a good idea after all.

The wind industry has had a good run. Two decades of stupidity from the governments that have just about given them a free rein to do what they like in rural Scotland. Westminster is maybe waking up (we live in hope but signs are promising) as the costs for this escalate and burden the consumer even more. However, given the comments by utterly clueless Stephen Gethins MSP (former sidekick to Fergus Ewing) the Scottish government has its head as firmly in the sand as it always has. It has backed nearly twenty years of increasing environmental destruction and ignored its rural communities to benefit only the public money troughers.

With peanuts offered in compensation by the global investors communities are left with all the disbenefits.

How much money would make it ok? Liberal Democrats seem to think we can be bought. We'd say its way too late and NOTHING would be enough now.

Here we have the wind industry's go to consultancy firm.

Biggar Economics.

Graeme Blackett, founder of said company, has publicly supported the expansion of renewable energy in Scotland and has spent many years producing economic assessments in support of wind farm developments. Yet these reports repeatedly fail to account for the substantial costs imposed on those forced to live with the consequences of such schemes. Loss of property value, reduced marketability of homes, damage to landscapes, impacts on wildlife, industrialisation of rural communities and the burden of associated transmission infrastructure are routinely excluded or downplayed. An economic assessment that counts only the benefits claimed by developers while ignoring the costs borne by affected residents is not an objective evaluation.

Increasingly tourists are speaking out against the appalling ripping up of iconic landscapes by Big Energy. Tourists are the life blood of many rural communities and if they decline in numbers then how are people in remote areas expected to survive - or is that the masterplan?

The jobs promises we all know are 


Temporary at best and not there most of the time.

So take this windwash report with a bucket of salt and help us fight back against this industrial garbage. If we stop the powerlines we stopped this windy wish list too.

Please donate to help pay for the professional representation we need to fight against the Scottish government rubber stampers and the corporates who see us as an irritation and want to change our lives for the worst - forever.

Yesterday, we watched  𝐌𝐢𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐞𝐥 𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐤𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐁𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐉𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐬 giving evidence to the 𝐋𝐨𝐫𝐝𝐬 𝐄𝐧𝐯𝐢𝐫𝐨𝐧𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 & 𝐂𝐥𝐢𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐂𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐞 𝐒𝐞𝐥𝐞𝐜𝐭 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐦𝐢𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐞.
We had not realised that there were preceding meetings on the same subject - 'Dunkelflaute and the risks of electricity intermittency'.  What we intended to do was to hold yesterday's summary, go back on the others, and put what we believe has come out of those meetings - and the Public Accounts Committee and ESNZ meetings, too - into one comprehensive summary.
However, last night, we saw a Telegraph article referring to yesterday's meeting.  In our opinion, the headline in particular - 'Burnham to halt wind and solar subsidies in net zero climbdown' and, indeed, some of the text, gives a different and wholly incorrect perspective from that which was actually said at yesterday's meeting.
(Other - industry - media is more restrained.  And, already, there is loud muttering about investor confidence.  It takes only one incautious - and unqualified - remark to set off investors, we believe.  It may be that Shanks will have to offer that qualification.) 
As a result of all this, we have brought forward yesterday's summary - in the images.  This is the text of what Shanks actually said, in relation to the Chair raising the subject of CfDs.

'Pause before AR9' - he did not say AR9 is cancelled, postponed indefinitely, or even that it will not proceed in 2027.
'Look at whether we need' - this is exploratory language. The Government is considering whether more substantial changes are necessary. It has not yet announced what those changes will be.
'To make sure they work for consumers' - this identifies the stated objective of the review, not its eventual outcome.
A pause to review the terms of an auction is not necessarily a pause in the auction timetable itself.
That said, we think we may be seeing a slight sea change, but it is way too early to make that assessment.  
In 2024, we described Michael Shanks as 'articulate and personable' compared to the zealous style of Miliband.  And he is.  However, when we take into account everything we've posted in the last two years, and in particular, when we've noted Shanks' incaution in, for example, being 'roasted' on social media for his comments to Kathryn Porter (and other examples of rashness which some have said do not befit a Minister of State,) - the Scottish word 'gallus' came into our heads, frequently, whilst watching the meeting.
And so, having taken cognisance of what has been said at the previous meetings we referred to above, by all those involved in the grid's continued ability to 'keep the lights on', we will:
1.  Wait to see what actually transpires by way of changes to AR9 and the relevant dates.
2.  Carry on putting together, as cohesively as we can, those other meetings and documents - taking our time to do it as there is now quite a mass.  We will then run by experts in the field that which we end up with and will finally post the findings.  
But for now, much as we would all like to see an announcement saying that Burnham has halted wind and solar subsidies in a net zero climbdown - neither he, nor anyone in the government or the energy sector, has made such a claim.

records.title: Scottish Electricity Generating Stations
records.bodyText:
The Shetland HVDC converter system links the Shetland Islands to the mainland Great electricity grid for the first time.
Each converter location features a 320/132kV converter station at Upper Kergord (Shetland) and an HVDC switching/converter interface at Noss Head (Caithness) on the Scottish mainland.
Built using Hitachi Energy's HVDC Light Voltage Source Converter (VSC) technology as part of Europe's first multi-terminal HVDC system (connecting into the Caithness- Moray link).
The link operates at ±320 kV with a capacity of 600 MW across a 260 km subsea and underground route.
The project unlocked renewable energy by exporting power from the 443 MW Viking Wind Farm and improving local energy security on the islands. Previously Shetland had operated as an island grid network separate from national grid network.
The transmission link commissioning was completed and began operation in August 2024. 
To enable the subsea cable from Shetland to connect to the transmission grid network, involved the construction of a high voltage direct current (HVDC) switching station north of Wick in Caithness. The switching station connects to the HVDC system between Caithness and Moray, and will make use of capacity available in the Caithness - Moray Subsea Cable to allow onward connection to the existing onshore transmission network in Moray, with minimum new infrastructure.
The switching station allows the flow of electricity to be managed between three underground HVDC circuits one from a converter station at Spittal in Caithness, one from a converter station at Kergord in Shetland, and one to a converter station at Blackhillock in Moray.
A further 2GW subsea link is planned but the mainland needs to be upgraded before this proposal can progress.— at Shetland Islands, Scotland.

records.title: Scotland Against Spin
records.bodyText:
Scotsman letters
The chancellor says his budget “… kickstarts the long-term action required to get energy costs down for good”. If that is truly the object, a starting point might be more transparency about the cost of offshore wind, a technology in which Scotland plays a leading role, and which is too often presented as a route to cheaper electricity.
Offshore wind is routinely invoked as proof net zero can bring both cleaner power and lower bills. In Scotland, it is promoted as an opportunity of national significance, hailed as the “main driver” for new energy infrastructure such as SSEN’S Kintore to Tealing 400kv OHL. Yet the economics are less obliging than the public is led to believe. Gas-fired generation is generally accepted to have a capital cost of around £1 million per MW. Even conventional offshore wind is far more expensive than that, but floating wind belongs in another stratosphere. Equinor’s floating wind farm, Hywind Scotland, for example, is estimated at £8.8m per MW yet this much higher cost of floating wind is overlooked within offshore figures to give a rosier impression than the evidence justifies.
Offshore wind is treated as though more capacity must, by definition, mean lower prices. But if generation costs are this high and more than £70 billion is expected to be spent on the transmission infrastructure needed to connect offshore wind to the grid, how can consumers simply be asked to take it on trust that bills will fall? Those costs will not vanish. They will be borne by households and businesses in Scotland as elsewhere.
The budget promises: “Prioritising a cheaper energy mix and procuring new generation only where it lowers bills, benefits the system and can be accommodated by the grid.”
That is a sensible litmus test and should be applied with rigour to offshore wind in all its forms. Can new projects genuinely be shown to reduce costs once transmission, balancing and constraint costs are included? Can the grid absorb them without still more spending? These surely are crucial questions for a government serious about affordability.
The government’s own figures show gas no longer sets the wholesale electricity price as it once did. If that link is weak, yet electricity remains expensive, it becomes difficult to blame gas alone. Could the pressure on prices come from the cost of building, connecting and integrating offshore wind?
None of this is an argument against cleaner energy. But offshore wind, no less than any other major investment, should be judged by a simple standard: Does it deliver reliable power at a cost the country can afford?
Until ministers can show how exorbitantly expensive offshore wind, coupled with £70bn of network investment, can yield cheaper electricity, the numbers look more like a cost moved from one side of the ledger to the other.
Eileen West Banchory, Aberdeenshire 
The Scottish government is forever criticising the UK government. Well the chickens have well and truly come home to roost.
The Scottish government thought they just had to snap their fingers and they would get funding from the UK government for Scotland’s proposed flagship Acorn carbon capture and storage project at St Fergus gas terminal near Peterhead (your report, 3 November).
As The Scotsman revealed, only £12 million will be provided as a grant to the developers, not the already promised £200m grant.
Scottish politicians set their net zero target for 2045 since “Scotland leads the world”. Many would say towards bankruptcy. No other country has pledged 2045. China has set its Net Zero target as “before 2060” but no date. India by 2070 and President Donald J Trump has put a huge question mark on USA Net Zero 2050 as he pledges “Drill, Baby, Drill”.
Caroline Rance, head of campaigns at Friends of Earth Scotland, said over a year ago: “Carbon capture technology has 50 years of failure behind it, so businesses, workers and the public are being sold a lie about its role in their future.”
Looks like she was correct. What a tangled green web politicians weave.
Clark Cross Linlithgow West Lothian

Turbines planned for a site near Lerwick will be fitted with lights to maintain flight safety for aircraft using Tingwall Airport.
New planning documents lodged for Statkraft’s Mossy Hill windfarm detail plans to use visible red lights for three of the eight turbines and infra-red lights, which are not visible to the naked eye, for all eight.

The Scotsman highlights growing industry fears that the SNP government is putting thousands of jobs at risk by failing to outline long-term ambitions for onshore wind capacity beyond 2030. Industry bodies, including the Scottish Onshore Wind Developers Forum, are warning that capping targets at 2030 risks undermining crucial supply chain investments and future energy planning
SNP ministers have been urged to draw up plans to triple Scotland’s onshore wind capacity by 2040 – with the industry saying it would support thousands of jobs and add billions to the economy.

It could result in more than 1,000 new wind farms being built across the countryside over the next 14 years.
